titleBlock.subtitle: All-possible NEB questions  •  short precise answers  •  exam shortcuts  •  worked examples

questions.question: Q1. Define electric field and find it for a point charge.
questions.answer: Electric field E is the force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q. For a point charge E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²), radially outward for +q and inward for −q.
questions.example: E of a 1 μC charge at 0.3 m: 9×10⁹×10⁻⁶/0.09 = 1×10⁵ N/C.

questions.question: Q2. Describe electric field lines and their properties.
questions.answer: Field lines represent the field; they start on + and end on −, never cross (field is single-valued), are denser where E is larger, and are perpendicular to conductors' surfaces. The number per unit area ∝ E.
questions.example: A dipole's lines curve from + to − outside.

questions.question: Q3. Find the field at the midpoint between +q at x=0 and −q at x=1 m.
questions.answer: Field from each at the midpoint is kq/0.5², both point in the same direction (from + to −): E = 2(kq/0.25) = 8kq/m² toward the negative charge.
questions.shortcut: Add the two (same direction) for +,− pair.

questions.question: Q4. Explain how Gauss's law can be used to find the field of a spherically symmetric charge.
questions.answer: By symmetry, E is radial and constant on a spherical Gaussian surface. Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ gives E(4πr²) = Q/ε₀ → E = Q/(4πε₀r²), the same as Coulomb's law. ▥ 20.1 Electric Field & Field Lines  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Electric Field vs Electric Potential Electric Field Line Rules (quick chart) ▣ 20.2–20.3 Gauss's Law & Applications
questions.example: A charged conducting sphere has E=0 inside, outside like a point charge.

questions.question: Q5. State Gauss's law and define electric flux.
questions.answer: Gauss's law: the net electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀. Electric flux Φ = ∫E·dA (units V·m).
questions.example: A closed surface with 2 C inside has Φ = 2/ε₀ V·m.

questions.question: Q6. Using Gauss's law find the field of an infinite charged plane of surface density σ.
questions.answer: Choose a pillbox Gaussian surface straddling the plane. Φ = E(2A) = σA/ε₀ → E = σ/(2ε₀). A surface charge on a conductor gives E = σ/ε₀ just outside.
questions.example: Double-sheet gives σ/ε₀, half for each sheet.

questions.question: Q7. Using Gauss's law find the field of an infinite line charge of linear density λ.
questions.answer: Use a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L. Flux = E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ → E = λ/(2πε₀r), radially outward.
questions.example: Field falls as 1/r for a line charge.

questions.question: Q8. Find the field just outside a charged conducting plate with σ = 4×10⁻⁶ C/m².
questions.answer: For a conductor, E = σ/ε₀ = 4×10⁻⁶/(8.85×10⁻¹²) ≈ 4.5×10⁵ N/C, perpendicular to the surface (E = 0 inside the conductor).

questions.question: Q9. Explain why the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero.
questions.answer: Free charges move until the excess resides on the surface; any internal field would push charges, contradicting equilibrium, so E_inside = 0. Also the surface is an equipotential and E is perpendicular to it.
questions.shortcut: E_inside = 0 ; charges live on the surface.
questions.example: A cavity inside a conductor also has zero field if it contains no charge.

questions.question: Q10. A uniformly charged solid sphere (total Q, radius R) — find E at r < R.
questions.answer: For r < R, Q_enc = Q(r/R)³; Gauss's law gives E(4πr²) = Q_enc/ε₀ → E = Qr/(4πε₀R³), proportional to r (zero at the centre). ▥ 20.2–20.3 Gauss's Law & Applications  —  Compare / Contrast Tables Gauss's Law: When It Helps PROFESSOR'S THEORY & VIVA BANK   — the kinds of theory a professor / examiner actually asks
questions.example: At the centre E = 0; at the surface it is maximum.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T1. Derive the field of a charged conducting sphere using Gauss's law.
theoryItems.answer: By spherical symmetry, E is radial and constant on a spherical Gaussian surface. For r < R, Q_enc = 0 → E = 0 (inside the conductor). For r > R, Q_enc = Q → E(4πr²) = Q/ε₀ → E = Q/(4πε₀r²), like a point charge at the centre.
theoryItems.example: A charged conducting sphere's interior is field-free.

theoryItems.question: [Derive] T2. Derive the field of an infinite line charge using Gauss's law.
theoryItems.answer: By cylindrical symmetry, E is radial and constant on a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r, length L: E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ → E = λ/(2πε₀r), falling as 1/r.
theoryItems.example: Field of a long wire falls off as 1/r.

theoryItems.question: [State] T3. State the formula for the electric field of a point charge and of a uniform infinite sheet.
theoryItems.answer: Point charge: E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²), radial. Uniform infinite sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀), constant and perpendicular to the sheet. A conducting surface just outside: E = σ/ε₀.

theoryItems.question: [State] T4. State Gauss's law and define electric flux.
theoryItems.answer: Gauss's law: the net electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀. Electric flux Φ = ∫E·dA (units V·m); it is the field 'flowing' through a surface.
theoryItems.example: A closed surface with 1 C inside has Φ = 1/ε₀ V·m.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T5. Explain electric field lines and their properties.
theoryItems.answer: Field lines are drawn so that the tangent gives the field direction and their density ∝ field strength; they start on positive charges and end on negative charges, never cross, and meet a conductor's surface at right angles. This is a qualitative way to map E.
theoryItems.shortcut: Lines: + → −, density ∝ E, never cross, ⟂ conductor.
theoryItems.example: A dipole's lines bow from + to −; a single charge's radiate out.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T6. Explain the field of a parallel-plate capacitor (conducting plates).
theoryItems.answer: Between two oppositely charged conducting plates, the fields add: E = σ/ε₀, uniform and perpendicular to the plates (outside, they cancel). This uniform field is why a capacitor stores energy and exerts a force on a charge between its plates.
theoryItems.shortcut: E = σ/ε₀ between the plates; uniform.
theoryItems.example: The field in an ideal parallel-plate capacitor is constant.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T7. Explain how Gauss's law is used for a charged infinite plane (sheet).
theoryItems.answer: Take a pillbox Gaussian surface straddling the sheet; by symmetry the flux through the two end caps is 2EA, the side contributes zero, and Q_enc = σA. So 2EA = σA/ε₀ → E = σ/(2ε₀) (per side; a conductor surface gives σ/ε₀ since both sides contribute).
theoryItems.example: A single infinite sheet gives σ/2ε₀ on each side.

theoryItems.question: [Explain] T8. Explain a Faraday cage and its shielding principle.
theoryItems.answer: A closed conducting enclosure redistributes its charges so that the internal electric field is zero; external fields are cancelled by induced surface charges. This is why a metal car or a shielded cable protects its interior from static/electrostatic fields.
theoryItems.example: A metal car in a thunderstorm protects the occupants.

theoryItems.question: [Why] T9. Why is the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium zero?
theoryItems.answer: Free charges in the conductor move until they cancel any internal field; if a field remained, it would continue to push charges, contradicting equilibrium. Hence E_inside = 0 and all excess charge sits on the surface (where the field is perpendicular).
theoryItems.example: A metal cavity shields its interior (Faraday cage).

theoryItems.question: [Viva] T10. Professor: 'Is Gauss's law more fundamental than Coulomb's law, or the other way round?'
theoryItems.answer: In vacuum Gauss's law (from Coulomb) is equivalent to Coulomb's law for point charges, but Gauss's law is more useful for symmetric charge distributions because it gives E directly from symmetry without integrating. In a medium, Gauss's law for D = ε₀E + P is more general (depends on free charge only).
theoryItems.shortcut: Both are equivalent; Gauss is more general for D.
theoryItems.example: Gauss's law is the shortcut for symmetric fields.

theoryItems.question: [Numerical] T11. An infinite line charge has λ = 2 μC/m. Find the field at r = 0.1 m.

▣ 20.1 Electric Field & Field Lines
Q1. Define electric field and find it for a point charge.
Answer:  Electric field E is the force per unit positive test charge: E = F/q. For a point charge E = (1/4πε₀)(q/r²), radially outward for +q and inward for −q.
⚡ Shortcut:  E = kq/r² (direction from + to −).
Example:  E of a 1 μC charge at 0.3 m: 9×10⁹×10⁻⁶/0.09 = 1×10⁵ N/C.
Q2. Describe electric field lines and their properties.

Answer:  Field lines represent the field; they start on + and end on −, never cross (field is single-valued), are denser where E is larger, and are perpendicular to conductors' surfaces. The number per unit area ∝ E.
⚡ Shortcut:  + → −; never cross; density ∝ E.
Example:  A dipole's lines curve from + to − outside.
Q3. Find the field at the midpoint between +q at x=0 and −q at x=1 m.
Answer:  Field from each at the midpoint is kq/0.5², both point in the same direction (from + to −): E = 2(kq/0.25) = 8kq/m² toward the negative charge.
⚡ Shortcut:  Add the two (same direction) for +,− pair.
Example:  For q = 1 μC: E = 8×9×10³ = 7.2×10⁴ N/C.
Q4. Explain how Gauss's law can be used to find the field of a spherically symmetric charge.
Answer:  By symmetry, E is radial and constant on a spherical Gaussian surface. Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀ gives E(4πr²) = Q/ε₀ → E = Q/(4πε₀r²), the same as Coulomb's law.
⚡ Shortcut:  Spherical symmetry → E·A = Q_enc/ε₀ ; A = 4πr².
Example:  A charged conducting sphere has E=0 inside, outside like a point charge.

Q5. State Gauss's law and define electric flux.
Answer:  Gauss's law: the net electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀: ∮E·dA = Q_enc/ε₀. Electric flux Φ = ∫E·dA (units V·m).
⚡ Shortcut:  Φ = Q_enc/ε₀.
Example:  A closed surface with 2 C inside has Φ = 2/ε₀ V·m.
Q6. Using Gauss's law find the field of an infinite charged plane of surface density σ.
Answer:  Choose a pillbox Gaussian surface straddling the plane. Φ = E(2A) = σA/ε₀ → E = σ/(2ε₀). A surface charge on a conductor gives E = σ/ε₀ just outside.
⚡ Shortcut:  Sheet: σ/2ε₀ ; conductor surface: σ/ε₀.
Example:  Double-sheet gives σ/ε₀, half for each sheet.
Q7. Using Gauss's law find the field of an infinite line charge of linear density λ.
Answer:  Use a cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L. Flux = E(2πrL) = λL/ε₀ → E = λ/(2πε₀r), radially outward.
⚡ Shortcut:  Cylinder: E = λ/(2πε₀r).
Example:  Field falls as 1/r for a line charge.
Q8. Find the field just outside a charged conducting plate with σ = 4×10⁻⁶ C/m².
Answer:  For a conductor, E = σ/ε₀ = 4×10⁻⁶/(8.85×10⁻¹²) ≈ 4.5×10⁵ N/C, perpendicular to the surface (E = 0 inside the conductor).
⚡ Shortcut:  E = σ/ε₀ outside a conductor.
Example:  ≈ 4.5×10⁵ N/C outward.
Q9. Explain why the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is zero.

Answer:  Free charges move until the excess resides on the surface; any internal field would push charges, contradicting equilibrium, so E_inside = 0. Also the surface is an equipotential and E is perpendicular to it.
⚡ Shortcut:  E_inside = 0 ; charges live on the surface.
Example:  A cavity inside a conductor also has zero field if it contains no charge.
Q10. A uniformly charged solid sphere (total Q, radius R) — find E at r < R.
Answer:  For r < R, Q_enc = Q(r/R)³; Gauss's law gives E(4πr²) = Q_enc/ε₀ → E = Qr/(4πε₀R³), proportional to r (zero at the centre).
⚡ Shortcut:  Inside: E ∝ r ; outside: E ∝ 1/r².
Example:  At the centre E = 0; at the surface it is maximum.

▹ Explain  (working / principle / application)
[Explain] T5. Explain electric field lines and their properties.

Answer:  Field lines are drawn so that the tangent gives the field direction and their density ∝ field strength; they start on positive charges and end on negative charges, never cross, and meet a conductor's surface at right angles. This is a qualitative way to map E.

[Why] T9. Why is the electric field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium zero?

Answer:  Free charges in the conductor move until they cancel any internal field; if a field remained, it would continue to push charges, contradicting equilibrium. Hence E_inside = 0 and all excess charge sits on the surface (where the field is perpendicular).

[Viva] T10. Professor: 'Is Gauss's law more fundamental than Coulomb's law, or the other way round?'

Answer:  In vacuum Gauss's law (from Coulomb) is equivalent to Coulomb's law for point charges, but Gauss's law is more useful for symmetric charge distributions because it gives E directly from symmetry without integrating.
